title: Kojiki
abstract: The "Kojiki" 古事記 (Record of Ancient Matters) is a mythohistorical text completed that chronicles the Age of the Gods, the founding of the Japanese empire, and the deeds of legendary and historical emperors and empresses up to the seventh century CE. According to the text's preface, Empress Genmei 元明天皇 (r. 707–715) commissioned the chronicle to be compiled by the courtier Ō no Yasumaro 太安万侶 (d. 723) in 711 CE. Yasumaro credits an individual named Hieda no Are 稗田阿礼 (ca. eighth century) as an assistant, possibly a woman trained in the Sarume ritualist clan, who recited oral histories and previous texts. The manuscript is written in Man'yōgana, a system for transcribing ancient Japanese phonetically through the use of Chinese characters, and its content is divided into three volumes. Book One covers myths recounting the Age of the Gods, including the creation of the universe and successive generations of kami and their production of various natural phenomena. It is in this section that the Three Noble Children, most importantly the sun goddess and imperial ancestress Amaterasu. Book Two chronicles the reigns of legendary emperors, beginning with the founding Emperor Jinmu and ending with Emperor Ōjin; Book Three turns to chronicle emperors whose reigns are supported by historical evidence, from Emperor Nintoku in the fourth century to Empress Suiko (r. 593–628). At the time of compilation, the Kojiki chiefly served as official textual support for the imperial lineage's divine right to rule and the authority of the Yamato state, the primacy of the imperial kami, the strategic inclusion and subordination of the noble clans of the Yamato court and their anestral deities, and the expansion of imperial lands through conquest. Just a few years later in 720 CE, another imperially commissioned mythohistorical text titled the "Nihon Shoki" (Chronicles of Japan) was completed; written in authoritative Classical Chinese and much more extensive and detailed, the Nihon Shoki largely overshadowed the Kojiki in official use and scholarly significance. However, the Kojiki remained revelant to the shrine priesthood, in particular to the priests of the Grand Shrines of Ise and the Urabe ritualist clan, who both preserved their own manuscripts with distinct annotations and commentary. The earliest extant copy of the Kojiki dates to the fourteenth-century Shinpukuji manuscript, compiled by Buddhist monks based on both Ise- and Urabe-lineage texts. In the seventeenth century, new printing technologies made the Kojiki available for reading by the masses. At the same time, Kokugaku (literally "National Learning," often translated as "Nativist") scholars sought to rediscover a unique and superior Japanese identity predating continental influences from ancient sources. Participants in this project—led by the "Great Four" intellectual lineage of Kada no Azumamaro 荷田春満, Kamo no Mabuchi 賀茂真淵, Motoori Norinaga 本居宣長, and Hirata Atsutane 平田篤胤—argued that both the content and the manner in which the Kojiki, now appreciated as an ur-text, was written provided vital evidence of the lost "Ancient Way" of Japan. The "Kojikiden," a forty-four-volume philological commentary on the Kojiki, is considered to be Norinaga's magnum opus and was instrumental in the resurgence of scholarly and political interest in the text as a source of historical fact, instead of legend, allegory, or literature. As such, the Kojiki took on greater sacred significance, eclipsing the Nihon Shoki in relevance. The modern Meiji state effectively canonized the Kojiki as a national document that established the divine rule of the emperor and highlighted the importance of the unification of rites and rule. See entry on State Shinto. Today, the Kojiki lies at the core of the Shinto textual canon. Kojiki studies continue at Shinto universities and shrines, and many mythic episodes (e.g., the tale of the Heavenly Grotto) are retold and reimagined in a variety of popular media including literature, comic books, animation, and video games.

title: Modernization of the rural handicraft industry in modern China: a case study of the hand-loom weaving industry
abstract: Industrialization represents the core of modernization, and the modernization of the handicraft industry in modern China provides a valuable empirical case for understanding industrialization in late-developing economies. This article takes the rural hand-loom weaving industry in modern China as the research subject to examine its modernization and inherent characteristics. Initiated in the aftermath of the Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), this modernization drive underwent two distinct phases: an initial upsurge and a subsequent setback. Propelled by imported foreign yarn and new weaving machinery, rural hand-loom weaving evolved from a marginal rural sideline into a large-scale production sector. Nevertheless, this developmental trajectory was abruptly halted by the global economic crisis of the 1930s and the outbreak of the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression. Marked by local cultural tradition, multi-dimensional factors, the interdependence of cities and the countryside, as well as the adoption of technological innovation and an expanding market, the modernization of the hand-loom weaving industry represents an unfinished path of “semi-industrialization.” This unique developmental path not only demonstrates the inherent potential of rural handicraft modernization in modern China but also exposes the profound challenges embedded in the Chinese countryside’s social and economic transformation.

title: Import restriction as a means of maintaining macroeconomic stability: Evidence from the Japanese experience of monetary and financial regulation
abstract: Aim. To reveal the role of import restriction in maintaining a stable national currency exchange rate through the regulation of export-import operations, using Japan’s development during a period of high economic growth as an example. Objectives. To analyze alternative measures for maintaining financial stability, including import restriction, which allows for effective management of the exchange rate; to examine the Japanese experience of maintaining the national currency exchange rate at a consistently high level over a long period, which has proven its viability and effectiveness. Methods. Using general scientific methods of cognition, comparison, and an institutional approach to the analysis of economic processes, the policy of state regulation of macroeconomic indicators through key rate management and the use of import restriction mechanisms to maintain a stable national currency exchange rate is examined, including the example of macroeconomic regulation in Japan in the second half of the 20th century. Results. Maintaining a stable national currency exchange rate is considered in the article as a measure aimed at combating inflation and as a less painful alternative to a strong increase in the key rate. The study and comparison of approaches to the problem of ensuring macroeconomic stability in Russia and Japan made it possible to identify differences in the national specifics of public administration problems in the financial sphere and to form an understanding of the factors contributing to the most favorable results of the process of maintaining a sustainable exchange rate over a long period. An important place among these factors, in addition to the policy of raising the key rate actively implemented in modern Russia, is occupied by the quite successful, as shown in the article, Japanese practice of regulating export-import operations. At the same time, a policy of import containment can become a key element in ensuring macroeconomic stability and maintaining a sustainable national currency exchange rate. Conclusions. Containing imports through quotas and other tariff and non-tariff restrictive measures contributes to stabilizing the national currency exchange rate and prevents depreciation of the national currency even under conditions of increased demand for foreign currency and a tendency toward rising inflation expectations. Unlike monetary measures, in which a floating national currency exchange rate serves as one of the main levers for balancing exportimport flows and at the same time is subject to sharp fluctuations, the methodology of administrative import containment makes it possible to achieve stability of the national currency exchange rate and helps keep inflation under control. As a result, it becomes possible to have a low key rate, allowing the country’s economy to develop dynamically with the active use of available credit resources

title: Performing Beauty: Itōkochōen, Kabuki Actors, and the Marketing of Lead-Free Cosmetics in Meiji Japan
abstract: This article examines how a consumer health crisis transformed cosmetics marketing in Japan’s emerging beauty industry. By the late nineteenth century, the dangers of lead-based oshiroi (white face powder) were widely recognized, particularly among kabuki actors who suffered visibly from occupational poisoning. Although manufacturers experimented with lead-free alternatives, contemporary observers repeatedly judged them inferior to conventional powders, revealing that safer cosmetics required not only scientific innovation but an acceptable substitute for an established and culturally desirable product. Itōkochōen sought to resolve this problem with Misono Oshiroi, a lead-free formulation distinguished by scientific authentication, imperial association, and an ambitious actor-centered marketing campaign. Through serialized advertorials, promotional booklets, and newspaper campaigns, kabuki actors drew on their professional expertise in cosmetics and firsthand experience of poisoning to translate medical beauty knowledge into practical instruction. The campaign reconfigured an Edo-period relationship between kabuki and commercial beauty for a market increasingly organized around hygiene, scientific expertise, and female consumption. In doing so, Itōkochōen demonstrates how Japanese firms modernized established commodities by combining product innovation with culturally specific forms of commercial persuasion.

title: Engishiki
abstract: The Engishiki 延喜式 ("Procedures of the Engi Era") is a tenth-century 50-volume legal code that includes 10 volumes pertaining specifically to Shinto shrines, their deities, the ritual calendar, and ritual manuals. During the period that Japan was governed under the ritsuryō legal system, adapted from Chinese legal codes heavily influenced by Confucianism and Legalism, shiki (as in the Engi shiki) provided detailed instructions for how to enact the laws of the land. The text was commissioned by Emperor Daigo 醍醐天皇 (r. 897–930) in 905 (year 5 of the Engi reign period, 901–923) and compiled over several decades under the leadership of two court officials from the powerful regent Fujiwara clan: Fujiwara Tokihira 藤原時平 (871–909) and Fujiwara Tadahira 藤原忠平 (880–949). Although the bulk of the manuscript was completed and presented to the emperor in 927, it underwent extensive revisions and did not go into effect until 967. Although many changes to the legal system in Japan were made over the centuries, particularly after military rule by the shogunate was established in the twelfth century, the Engishiki remained an important legal document until the Meiji Restoration in 1868. The Engishiki's ritual prescriptions only officially pertained to a select number of shrines that received imperial support and were overseen by the Jingikan 神祇官 (Department of Divinities). Chief among them were shrines connected to the imperial family, such as the Grand Shrines of Ise, and the oldest and most powerful clans in the Yamato court. Volumes 1 and 2 lay out the annual calendar of rites, organized by month in the lunarsolar calendar. Volume 3 covers extraordinary rites that would be performed on certain occasions, such as the outbreak of an epidemic or groundbreaking for a new building. Volume 4 deals with the rites held at the Grand Shrines of Ise, where the imperial ancestress Amaterasu was enshrined, while Volumes 5 and 6 concern the rites and procedures observed by imperial princesses at Ise and the Kamo shrines in Kyoto. Volume 7 describes the enthronement rituals performed upon the installation of a new emperor. Volume 8 includes transcriptions of the prayer formulas (norito 祝詞) recited during various rites. Volumes 9 and 10 record a registry of important shrines and their deities across Japan; this section, directly referred to as the Engishiki Jinmyōchō 延喜式神名帳, lists 2,861 shrines and 3,132 deities that received state patronage. The other 40 volumes concern penal, administrative, and supplementary laws. Because kami worship was a matter overseen by a court department (i.e., the Jingikan), there is some intersection between that department and other departments (Daijōkan). Shinto does not have a scriptural or hagiographic canon similar to other "major" or "world" religions. However, the Engishiki is considered a canonical work within Shinto tradition and scholarship because it archives rare historical and practical details of rituals, shrines, and their enshrined deities. The document also demonstates the central role that the imperial cult played in the legitimization and administration of the emperor and his court. Today, shrines included in the Jinmyōchō registry (Shikinaisha 式内社) claim a certain level of historical status and importance based on their ranking. The answers provided in the poll below focus narrowly on the first 10 volumes of the Engishiki explicitly pertaining to kami worship. However, notes are provided to help give context relevant to other volumes in the document.

title: Women Leadership in Japanese Politics and Gender Manifestation in Policies
abstract: This article analyzes the complex state of female political leadership in Japan, emphasizing the tension between democratic progress and persistent socio-political traditionalism. Sanae Takaichi's historic election as first female Prime Minister of Japan in October 2025 represents a major milestone in descriptive representation, but it has not yet produced substantive, policy-based gender equality. Tracing developments from early imperial leadership through the restrictive Meiji-era ie household system and post-1945 constitutional guarantees, the study examines the systemic barriers that continue to limit women's role in national decision-making. Key obstacles include male-dominated, hereditary political networks that control the “three bans”: jiban constituency base, kanban name recognition, and kaban campaign funding. As a result, despite local gains in municipal politics, women remain underrepresented nationally, holding only 14.6 percent of House of Representatives seats as of February 2026. The paper ultimately shows that symbolic leadership breakthroughs can coexist with elite efforts to preserve conservative political structures rather than drive meaningful social change. Keywords: Female political leadership; Japan politics; Sanae Takaichi; ‘three bans’ (jiban; kanban; kaban); Sixth Basic Plan on Gender Equality

venue.name: International Journal of Law Politics and Governance

title: Public Bathhouses in Japan: Information Space, Gendered Economy, and the Transformation of Social Life
abstract: This article examines the socio-economic evolution of Japanese public bathhouses (sento) as dual spaces of the gendered economy and cultural exchange. Rooted in Shinto and Buddhist purification rituals, sento evolved from medieval religious sites into Edo-era commercial hubs that fostered communal ties and served as informal “information libraries” for commoners. Mixed bathing (konyoku), initially driven by economic necessity, became increasingly associated with eroticism through the labor of female attendants (yuna), revealing a gendered economy in which women’s bodies were commodified to sustain male productivity. During the Meiji period, modernization redefined sento as hygienic institutions, yet they persisted as resilient cultural symbols amid urbanization. A comparative analysis with Roman baths and Chinese teahouses highlights how sento connect religion, commerce, and gender relations while continually adapting to shifting notions of public and private life without losing their distinctive social functions.

title: Transplanting a socio-cultural innovation: Life insurance in Meiji Japan
abstract: This study examines the establishment of a domestic life insurance industry in Meiji Japan from a comparative perspective. Life insurance represented a socio-cultural innovation that emerged in the context of Western modernization. Its rapid adaptation to Japan’s socio-economic and cultural environment was remarkable. To uncover the underlying mechanisms of this process, the study addresses three key questions: how foreign insurers, the government, and domestic entrepreneurs contributed to the establishment of the industry; how the market was developed as seen in the occupational and regional distribution of early customers and the changes in product composition; and how domestic entrepreneurs sought to convince policyholders of the moral legitimacy of life insurance, the fairness of their offerings, and their ability and willingness to fulfil their long-term contractual obligations. The findings are contrasted with experiences in other countries, revealing both differences and similarities that can be linked to variations and commonalities in national context.

title: Tenrikyo
abstract: Tenrikyo 天理教 is one of the oldest and, despite demographic shifts and an aging membership, one of the largest of Japan's "new religions." In many ways, the early history of Tenrikyo reflects the history of Japan's modernization across the late-nineteenth and early-twentieth centuries, as the religion continually adapted and redefined itself in order to both respond to changing social needs and cultural expectations. For example, as Japan's Edo era drew to a close, early Tenrikyo offered hope for an egalitarian future to people ready to move on from feudalism, yet also anxious about the tumultuous times that would accompany the fall of the military government. Later, as the Meiji government began to rapidly modernize, Tenrikyo offered hope and healing to rural populations left out from what was largely an urban modernization project. And, as Japanese politicians, intellectuals, and other social actors struggled to define what "religion" might look like in a Japanese context, and what role it should play in the modernized Japan, Tenrikyo leadership sought acceptance and recognition through trying to be a model "modern religion." A notable aspect of how Tenrikyo is structured, which helps to explain this flexibility and ability to adapt to different needs and contexts, is that this one religion is comprised of dozens of distinct networks, each of which has been shaped by their respective histories and contexts. While the heart of Tenrikyo lies in Jiba, the location the Foundress proclaimed was the birthplace of humanity, as well as in the administrative offices and departments built around Jiba that make up Tenrikyo Church Headquarters, this core is shared by networks of Tenri churches known as keitō, or "church lineage networks." Each of these church lineage networks is organized and defined by systems of familial and interpersonal connections, rather than by specific geography or demographics. Two Tenrikyo churches located on the same street, but established by members of different church lineages, in many ways might as well be on opposite sides of the world. In contrast, two churches may be hundreds of miles apart, but through shared history and family bonds actually maintain a strong connection and feel a shared sense of community and culture. While conducting fieldwork on Tenrikyo, I became affiliated with a grand church located in the heart of Tokyo, but which sat at the head of a network that extended across Japan and beyond. These networks complicate attempts to clearly define fieldsites and demographics: some of my fieldsites were urban, and others rural; some rich, and some in need; some home to small dwindling communities, others growing at surprising speeds. This entry is titled "Tenrikyo in Contemporary Japan" to reflect the diversity of fieldsites included in my analysis; but I think it is almost important to emphasize that this is still just one church lineage network among many. Though they are all ultimately overseen by Tenrikyo Church Headquarters, and all share Jiba as their spiritual home, each church lineage network is shaped by shared history, inherited social dynamics, and families both natal and found. --- My responses are informed by my time conducting fieldwork in Japan and, to a lesser extent, the US. Between 2017 and 2018, I spent just under one year conducting interviews and participant observation among multiple field sites within a particular church lineage network, with my primary fieldsite being the grand church at the head of that network, located in Tokyo, Japan. I returned in the summer of 2019 to conduct additional interviews and document potential changing trends or dynamics over that following year. Further updates and interviews have been facilitated remotely via Zoom, LINE, and various social media platforms.

title: A STUDY ON KAWAGUCHI CATHOLIC CHURCH IN OSAKA (PART 1) : THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE CHURCH FROM THE VIEWPOINT OF LAND USE
abstract: The Kawaguchi Catholic Church in Osaka was established by French priests of the Missions étrangères de Paris adjacent to the Kawaguchi foreign settlement. Analysis of diplomatic and administrative documents from the late Edo and early Meiji periods reveals that the church site was secured through the intervention of French vice-consul Joseph Lèques, who simultaneously ac-quired a former daimyō warehouse-residence for the French consulate. This study demonstrates that the founding of Kawaguchi Church was made possible by French diplomatic leverage at a time when Christianity remained officially prohibited in Japan, highlighting the entanglement of religious mission and consular authority.

title: JAPANESE CONSTITUTIONALISM: FROM THE MEIJI CONSTITUTION TO THE PACIFIST CONSTITUTION — RUPTURES, CONTINUITIES, AND TRANSFORMATIONS
abstract: Japanese constitutionalism constitutes an experience of national and constitutional transformation, marked by the transition from the imperial order established by the Meiji Constitution of 1889 to the Constitution of 1946, in force since 1947, founded upon popular sovereignty, fundamental rights, parliamentary government, constitutional supremacy, and pacifism. The significance of this subject lies in understanding how a constitutional order incorporates foreign influences, preserves elements of its historical identity, and confronts ruptures and processes of reconstruction. The research adopts a historical-legal, constitutional, and comparative approach, combining normative analysis, historical reconstruction, institutional examination, specialized scholarship, and historical documents. The comparison with the United States and France identifies processes of circulation, reception, adaptation, and reinterpretation of ideas, without establishing hierarchies among constitutional models. This study examines constitutional formation during the Meiji Restoration, the establishment of the 1889 Constitution, Taishō Democracy, the rise of ultranationalism and militarism, the rupture of 1945, the drafting of the postwar Constitution, and its contemporary challenges. It concludes that the Japanese specificity results from the interaction between constitutional continuity and institutional transformation. The formal continuity of the constitutional text since 1947 coexists with significant interpretive changes, particularly concerning Article 9, self-defense, national security, and fundamental rights. The Japanese experience, therefore, does not provide a model for constitutional transplantation, but rather a field for reflection on the legal limits, possibilities, and tensions involved in constitutional adaptation.

title: A Study of Kanji Words Containing ‘者’ in the “Eiwajii”
abstract: Building on Lee Ja-ho (2026), who identified the characteristics of the word forms of niji kanji + sha (二 字漢字+者) and estimated their patterns, this study extends the analysis to all cases of kanji notation + sha (漢字表記+者), including niji kanji + sha, and describes their characteristics from the perspective of word type. The results are as follows. First, ichiji kanji + sha (一字漢字 + 者) showed a roughly even distribution between word-form structures and phrase-form structures in terms of word formation. This is because many forms such as ‘吹者’ cannot be regarded as independent words; in many such cases, 者 functioned as a native Japanese element combined with テ or with a synonymous expression. Second, niji kanji + sha (二字漢字 + 者) showed approximately three times as many word-form structures as phrase-form structures. This is because many niji-kanji forms combined with 者 had already been established as lexical items. Third, among all cases of kanji notation + sha (漢字表記+者), the reading シャ was used more frequently for 者, followed by ‘ニン’. This tendency is related to the growing dominance of 者 as a coined element denoting a person, replacing 人 during the late Edo and early Meiji periods.Fourth, sanji kanji + sha (三字漢字+者) and yoji kanji + sha (四字漢字+者) tend to consist of difficult lexical items, often involving technical terms such as -學 and -病. However, because the number of such examples is limited, detailed analysis and evaluation remain difficult. This study is significant in that it infers the word-form status of kanji notation + sha (漢字表記＋者), the only category in Eiwajii that does not follow the furigana notation method, and clarifies the linguistic characteristics of 漢字表記 and 者 through word-type analysis. Based on these findings, the relationship between kanji notation and furigana in “Eiwaji” can be expected to be revealed more concretely and clearly.

title: Distribution of publications that encourage success through the Career Success Guidebooks for Elementary School Graduates in Colonial Korea, 1920s: Publication background and contents of How to become successful just by graduating from elementary school and The success story of a Choseon youth
abstract: This study examined the publication of How to become successful just by graduating from elementary school in colonial Korea in 1922. This book mimicked the content of a book published in Japan in the early 1900s that offered advice on how to achieve success to elementary school graduates. And I examined The success story of a Choseon youth, published by the Japanese Government-General of Korea in 1927. This book emulates a book of success stories of business people published in Japan in the 1900s. Both books belong to the genre of success-promoting books published in Japan following the success boom of the 1900s. The ethos of social climbing during the early Meiji period was disseminated through translated editions of Self-Help. In the 1900s, the concept of success was disseminated through a series of publications that taught the methods for achieving it. In 1920s colonial Korea, books offering advice on how to achieve success were published. A translation of the book Self-Help was also published during this period. In short, I realized that the history of social climbing in Korea differed from that of Japan.

title: Memory Infrastructure and Historical Responsibility in Industrial Heritage - A Comparative Study of the Topf & Sons Place of Remembrance and the Sites of Japan’s Meiji Industrial Revolution -
abstract: 본 연구는 ‘기억 인프라’라는 개념을 통해 폭력의 역사와 결합된 산업유산을 고찰한다. 독일의 ‘기억의 장소 토프 운트 죄네-아우슈비츠의 소각로 제작자들’과 일본의 ‘메이지 일본의 산업혁명유산’, 특히 하시마(端島)와 산업유산정보센터를 장소성, 기록⋅증언, 전시∙해석, 운영 주체∙제도의 측면에서 비교한다. 토프 운트 죄네에서는 나치의 대량학살에 대한 기업의 책임이 가시화되는 반면, 하시마와 산업유산정보센터에서는 근대 산업화의 성취가 전면에 부각되고 강제동원의 역사는 제한적으로 제시된다. 이러한 차이는 두 사례에서 기억 인프라가 형성되고 제도화된 경로의 차이와도 맞물려 있다. 이를 통해 산업유산의 의미가 장소, 기록, 전시, 제도의 선택과 배치 및 그 관계 속에서 구성됨을 밝히고, 산업유산이 역사적 책임을 포괄하는 기억 인프라로 기능하기 위한 조건을 제시한다.

title: Devenir histórico del haiku proletario japonés y su recepción en lengua castellana: análisis y estudio
abstract: Japanese proletarian literature is a cultural and political phenomenon that began in the early 20th century. Its starting point is necessarily multiple and complex, and it was accelerated by various events, among which the following stand out: the incursion of Commodore Perry’s ships in 1853, the Meiji Restoration of 1868—which marked a complex and gradual opening between East and West—the Russo-Japanese War, the rapid process of industrialization, and finally, the difficult conditions of Japanese factory workers, a circumstance that fostered their interest in socialist thought. In this article, it will focus on the birth of the haiku that can be termed proletarian or socially conscious, through the プロレタリア俳句運動 (Puroretaria haijin dōmei, or Proletarian Haiku Poets Association) as a poetic response to the coercion and oppression of two forms of fanaticism, especially between 1920 and 1945: imperialist power (the government and the Emperor) and the control of poetic art exercised by Takahama Kyoshi and his circle and the journal Hototogisu, which did not eliminate the spirit of proletarian synergies as one of the various movements of the so-called “new rising haiku.” Despite repression, proletarian haiku did not disappear and transformed after 1945 into the 新俳句人連盟 (Shin haikujin renmei, or Federation of Haiku Poets) as the legacy of this libertarian movement, an association that continues to this day. Finally, in this article, it will highlight the limited attention and theoretical development of proletarian haiku in the West and analyze the results of a study on haiku translations into Spanish, as well as the limited reception of proletarian haiku in those translations.

title: An Alliance Made in Heaven: Religion, Literature and the Discovery of Interiority in Turn-of-the-Century East Asia
abstract: At the turn of the twentieth century, a fierce ideological battle was raging in Japan to define what it meant to be ‘the people’ and who controlled the interior space of each individual. In response to the Meiji government’s aggressive indoctrination of human interiority, religion and literature joined forces against oppressive power. This short essay is about a transnational and transreligious struggle for human interiority in Japan and Korea, discussing Christianity, the worship of nature, Tolstoyan religion and Tonghak in tandem. Through the seemingly disparate combination of Uemura Masahisa, Kunikida Doppo, and Yi Kwang-su, it will demonstrate the fluidity of the concept of religion and that religion was often an integral part of the thoughts and practices of those who did not appear overtly religious––and vice versa.

title: Victory, Riots, and Rejection: The Russo-Japanese War, Japanese Nationalism, and the Collapse of the Harriman-Katsura Memorandum
abstract: This paper examines railroad magnate E.H. Harriman’s failed bid to acquire control of the South Manchuria Railway following the Russo-Japanese War. The paper primarily draws on George Kennan’s contemporary account, E. H. Harriman's Far Eastern Plans (1917), as well as many scholarly sources about the Russo-Japanese War, the Treaty of Portsmouth, Meiji Japan, the Hibiya riots, and other relevant topics. Newspapers, photographs, and other primary sources are also incorporated. The paper argues that the collapse of the Harriman-Katsura memorandum was not due to a simple failure of negotiation. Instead, it was a collision between two positions that were fundamentally incompatible: American commercial capitalism, which viewed the railway as a business asset that could and should be sold and optimized for profit, and Japanese imperial nationalism, grown by the Meiji Restoration and intensified into anti-Western sentiment following Japan’s stunning victory over Russia in 1905. The Japanese victory over a major European power was the first of its kind in modern history, and with that, Japan did not want or see a need to share the spoils of its war with American capitalists. For the Japanese, the South Manchuria Trophy was a crucial trophy of a war that had cost them nearly 100,000 lives. The Hibiya riots of September 1905 showed the volatility of the Japanese public over the terms of the Treaty of Portsmouth. Foreign Minister Komura Jutarō's decision to oppose and ultimately block the memorandum showed a pragmatic assessment of the domestic political situation. Harriman built his career by rehabilitating and acquiring failing American railroads, and he assumed that Japan’s financial strain would compel them to comply. He was wrong. The collapse of the Harriman Memorandum marks a moment when new Japanese confidence, born of their military successes, prevented a joint U.S.-Japanese economic venture and set the stage for a strategic rivalry in East Asia.

title: Japan’s Identity and Its Separation from Asia
abstract: This paper argues that Japan's modern national identity developed through a cyclical process of orientation toward the West and Asia, unfolding across four phases: pre-modern participation in the Sinocentric order; the Meiji-era construction of a new identity through deliberate separation from Asia, exemplified by Fukuzawa Yukichi's Datsu-A Ron; interwar disillusionment following Japan's racial rejection at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, which drove a turn toward Pan-Asianism and the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere; and postwar reintegration into the Western order under American occupation. Rather than discarding earlier frameworks, each reorientation repurposed them, so that the hierarchical civilizational logic adopted during the Meiji period persisted even as Japan's stated allegiances shifted. This continuity, the paper contends, helps explain Japan's enduring Western alignment, its unresolved tensions with China and South Korea, and the contested legacy of empire shaping its regional relationships today.

title: Medicine, Religion, and Imperialism: Japanese Women Doctors in China (1900–1945)
abstract: The establishment of modern medical systems in Meiji Japan opened new pathways for women to enter the medical profession, even as their authority remained constrained by prevailing gender norms. While most of these women doctors practised within Japan, some pursued medical work in China, engaging in transnational practices that have received little scholarly attention. This article examines these activities through the lens of gendered medical diplomacy, in which medical care, humanitarian service, and moral authority functioned as gendered modes of imperial engagement. Through the careers of Maejima Keiko (who arrived in Hangzhou in 1901) and Ikenaga Hideko (who worked in Beijing during the 1930s and 1940s), it traces how this form of diplomacy evolved across distinct imperial contexts. Maejima’s practice, which was conducted through Buddhist networks during a period of relatively informal Japanese expansion, highlights an early phase of Sino–Japanese medical exchange involving women doctors. Ikenaga’s later work, which was shaped by Christian missionary networks and wartime institutions, reveals how women’s medical authority operated within more explicitly imperial structures. Together, these cases show how transnational medical practice loosened gender constraints on women’s professional and personal lives while remaining deeply embedded in imperial power relations in modern East Asia.

title: JAPANESE PHOTOGRAPHY: THE FORMATION OF A NATIONAL TRADITION
abstract: The article examines the formation of Japanese photography in the second half of the nineteenth century. It focuses on the Meiji era – a period of sweeping reforms and openness to the world, when Western technologies rapidly permeated Japanese culture. Drawing on the works of early photographers such as Ueno Hikoma, Shimooka Renjō, Ichiki Shirō, and others, the study explores how foreign technical innovations were combined with local artistic trad itions. Particular attention is paid to the influence of the aesthetic principles of wabi-sabi, mono-no-aware, and Japanese minimalism. It is demonstrated that the synthesis of Western methods and Japanese artistic vision became the foundation for the formation of a national school of photography. The influence of traditional aesthetics on the Provoke movement in the twentieth century and on contemporary digital media is also considered. The article shows that the combination of Western technique and national aesthetics shaped a distinctive visual language of Japanese photography that remains relevant in modern culture.

title: Religious Ethos and Political Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of the Role of Religion in Shaping the National Ideologies of Japan and Singapore
abstract: Abstract The purpose of the present study was to identify the mechanisms of the functioning of religious ethos in the political discourse of Japan and Singapore. The methodology combined political science, cultural studies, religious studies, and historical-genetic analysis. The findings showed that Japan developed a distinctive model of religious-political interaction based on Shintoism as a sacralised foundation of statehood. During the Meiji period, State Shinto legitimised political authority and national unity, while after 1945, religious symbols continued to influence national consciousness despite official secularism. In Singapore, religious pluralism contributed to a model of “managed harmony,” in which Confucian ethics, adapted to modern conditions, supported civic cohesion. The state regulated the religious sphere to preserve social stability. Comparative analysis demonstrated that both countries used religion as an instrument of political integration, although through different institutional mechanisms. Confucian traditions were particularly significant in both contexts, but acquired different political interpretations. The study concluded that religion remains an important component of contemporary national ideologies, adapting to modernisation and globalisation without losing cultural identity. The findings may inform political planning in culturally diverse societies.

title: Kyoto's Universities at War, 1937-1945 : Using Institutional History, Addressing Institutional Responsibility
abstract: The development of Japan's university sector was a key factor in Japan's modernization process after the Meiji Restoration. The period from the 1870s to 1940s was also a period of Japanese imperialism, and from the 1930s, militarism. As a result, many of Japan's oldest and most prestigious universities, both national/public and private, made important scientific, social, and intellectual contributions to imperialism and militarism. This article examines how three prestigious universities in Kyoto—Kyoto University, Ritsumeikan University, and Doshisha University—have presented their wartime roles in university histories. These universities—a national (formerly imperial) university, a private secular university, and a private religious university, respectively—constitute a useful microcosm of the broader higher education sector in the 1930s. Furthermore, Kyoto's relative lack of wartime destruction during air raids forces the universities to focus on their active roles in the war effort rather than passive victimhood. The article analyzes the universities' histories as presented in university websites, official university histories, on-campus exhibitions, and the research of individual academics and employees. It demonstrates how a university produces multiple versions of its own history, presenting quite different images of its past. Understanding these differences requires identifying the actors within the university who produced the history, for what purpose, and how they disseminate the narrative. Universities must balance the desire to use "history for promotion" while remaining faithful to historical honesty, accuracy, and scholarship regarding an extremely divisive period of national Japanese history.

title: A Comparative Study of Longing, Desire and Loss in 19th-century English and Japanese Love Poetry
abstract: The language of love transcends national boundaries. Although love and emotional conflict are universal human experiences, they are expressed differently across cultures and literary traditions. Different poets articulate longing, desire and loss with varying intensity, mood, imagery, and cultural identity. However, despite these differences in expression, the underlying emotions remain fundamentally the same, reflecting a shared human experience beyond geographical and linguistic boundaries. This paper offers a comparative study of nineteenth-century Japanese and English love poetry, investigating how emotions such as longing, desire and loss transcended national boundaries while being shaped by distinct cultural and historical contexts. Set against the backdrop of Meiji modernization in Japan and the industrial, moral, and social transformations of nineteenth-century England, the study examines how poets articulated similar emotional experiences through different moods, intensities, and cultural identities. The study argues that while the expression of emotion varies across literary traditions, the fundamental human experience of love and emotional conflict remains universal. Through close reading and cultural-historical analysis, the paper examines select poems by Masaoka Shiki, Yosano Akiko, and Ochiai Naobumi, alongside poems by Christina Rossetti, A. E. Housman, and Rupert Brooke.

title: Modern-Day Kaidan: Japanese Horror Storytelling as Popular Culture
abstract: This article explores the history and modern developments of the Japanese horror storytelling tradition known as kaidan. It traces its origins from the first period of mass popularity in the Edo period, through the scepticism that permeated the social climate of the Meiji period, to the 20th century, when the introduction of film and television enabled kaidan to diversify into different media. The 1990s are examined as an especially transformative period when kaidan entered the mainstream through the popularity of J-Horror, TV shows and dedicated books and magazines that invited readers to experience the narratives firsthand by venturing out to haunted locations. Along this rich horror mediascape, oral storytelling also experienced a resurgence, taking the form of competitions, live performances and themed bars hosting kaidan events. The author explores these phenomena using media analysis, field observations and interviews.

title: Sodobni kaidan: japonsko pripovedništvo grozljivk kot popularna kultura
abstract: This article explores the history and modern developments of the Japanese horror storytell-ing tradition known as kaidan. It traces its origins from the first period of mass popularity in the Edo period, through the scepticism that permeated the social climate of the Meiji period, to the 20th century, when the introduction of film and television enabled kaidan to diversify into different media. The 1990s are examined as an especially transformative period when kaidan entered the mainstream through the popularity of J-Horror, TV shows and dedicated books and magazines that invited readers to experience the narratives firsthand by venturing out to haunted locations. Along this rich horror mediascape, oral storytelling also experienced a resurgence, taking the form of competitions, live performances and themed bars hosting kaidan events. The author explores these phenomena using media analysis, field observations and interviews.

title: The Emperor's Modernity: A Narrative Review of the Meiji Restoration from Norman's Emergence to Ravina's Century
abstract: The Meiji Restoration---the 1868 overthrow of Japan's samurai order and the state-led modernization that followed---is modern history's most consequential non-Western revolution, and its historiography a century-long argument about what kind of revolution it was. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Norman's 1940 emergence study, Craig's 1961 Choshu, Harootunian's 1970 political consciousness, Beasley's 1972 Restoration, Akamatsu's 1972 revolution and counter-revolution, Totman's 1980 bakufu collapse, Gluck's 1985 modern myths, Hall's 1991 Cambridge nineteenth century, Jansen's 2000 Making of Modern Japan, Gordon's 2003 modern history, Howell's 2005 geographies of identity, and Ravina's 2017 nations of the world. The synthesis is organized around three themes: collapse, in which the Tokugawa order fell to internal fiscal failure, external pressure, and samurai reformism; construction, in which the Meiji state built conscription, industrialization, and an emperor-centered ideology; and interpretation, in which the restoration was read as bourgeois revolution, top-down reform, or plural modernity. It is concluded that Meiji is modernization's laboratory---its speed unmatched, its costs real---and that the historiography's arc tracks the twentieth century's own theories of how modernity happens.

title: Examining the Relationship Between Tatara Iron Production and Grassland Distribution in Western Japan: An Open Geospatial Approach to Historical Landscape Analysis
abstract: Abstract. In western Japan, traditional tatara iron production has long been associated, both in historical narratives and in early ecological work, with the persistence of grassland landscapes. This view was stated by Itow (1962), but the inferred link has rarely been examined with spatially explicit data. We examine the spatial relationship between tatara iron production sites and grassland distribution in Tottori Prefecture using an integrated open-source geospatial workflow. The two data layers are temporally offset by design: tatara sites spanning from the medieval period to the mid-Meiji era, while the earliest spatially explicit municipality-level grassland record—the 1950 World Agricultural Census—captures the “landscape memory” of those activities roughly half a century after the cessation of large-scale tatara. Census tables were digitised using AI-assisted, sub-page table extraction. Tatara site locations (N = 562) were compiled from the Tottori Prefecture cultural-heritage WebGIS. Geology, basin structure, and DEM-derived terrain were processed with GeoPandas, rasterio, scipy, and rasterstats; OLS regression, model comparison, and DBSCAN clustering were implemented in statsmodels and scikit-learn. Tatara sites form well-defined production districts in the granitic Hino River basin, but grassland is most strongly predicted by elevation, with tatara density adding only modest marginal information. The count × slope interaction is significantly negative, indicating that the apparent tatara–grassland association weakens sharply in steep terrain. We interpret these patterns as evidence that both phenomena occupy the same mountain environmental niche, consistent with a niche-construction reading rather than a direct landscape-transformation interpretation.

title: In memory of Professor Akira Nakamura (1940–2026), Meiji University, Tokyo, Japan
“World Literature” and the Civilizational Consciousness of Meiji Buddhism: Ashizu Jitsuzen and Genuine Philosophy of Killing and Activating Freedom
abstract: Following the Meiji Restoration, Japanese Buddhism underwent a profound transformation as it confronted the rise of State Shinto, the spread of Christianity, and the emergence of modern concepts such as “religion” “civilization” and “philosophy”. Against this background, this paper examines the concept of “world literature” (sekai bungaku 世界文学) within the intellectual context of Meiji Buddhism, with particular attention paid to Ashizu Jitsuzen’s (1850–1921) discussion of the concept in Genuine Philosophy of Killing and Giving Life (1890). The paper first explores the formation of the modern religious order in Meiji Japan and the challenges Buddhism faced in redefining its social and cultural legitimacy. It then examines Ashizu’s religious thought and public activities, focusing on how he articulated the significance of Buddhism within the emerging modern public sphere and global order of knowledge, as well as the relationship between his notion of “world literature” and contemporary discussions of religion, civilization, and the emerging discourse of “world religions”. This paper argues that Ashizu’s notion of “world literature” sought to demonstrate that Buddhist scriptures possessed systematic structures of knowledge, interpretive methods, and mechanisms of transmission, enabling Buddhism to transcend national and regional boundaries and claim universal significance. At the same time, it shows that Ashizu regarded the realization of this potential as requiring Buddhist practitioners to develop new forms of learning, practice, and global propagation. By examining the tension between the inherited textual resources of the Buddhist tradition and modern Buddhism’s efforts toward global engagement, this paper reveals how Meiji Buddhist thinkers sought to reconstruct Buddhism’s position within a rapidly changing modern world order.

title: The Transformation of the Court and the Sino-Japanese War
abstract: This paper examines the personnel reorganization within the Japanese imperial court that occurred amid the political upheaval of the mid-1930s—namely, the resignation of Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Makino Nobuaki and the February 26 Incident. Furthermore, its impact on the decision-making structure during the early stages of the Second Sino-Japanese War is analyzed. Centered on Lord Keeper Yuasa Kurahei, this new court leadership that emerged after Makino’s departure exhibited a markedly diminished grip on the political situation, revealing a serious functional vacuum. This leadership adopted a passive stance during the collapse of Ugaki Kazushige’s attempt to form a cabinet. Moreover, despite the North China Separation Movement and the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese War, it failed to adequately check or restrain the unilateral assertiveness of the military, thereby exposing the limits of its capacity for political mediation. In contrast, Emperor Hirohito emerged as an active agent of counsel and decision-making, directly intervening in pressing matters of state. The Emperor personally corrected errors of political judgment made by the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal so as to forestall controversy over interference in the prerogative of supreme command. He took the initiative—for instance, by directly instructing that the operational outlook of the Army and Navy General Staffs be shared with Prime Minister Konoe—in an effort to mitigate the chronic structural defect of the Meiji constitutional order: the disjunction between state administration and the supreme command. Likewise, immediately following the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, he sought to pursue peace negotiations because of possible Soviet military intervention. Nevertheless, he was unable to prevent the full-scale, protracted escalation of the Sino-Japanese War despite his efforts at policy coordination through the convening of the Imperial Conference in January 1938.

title: Places and affects in the “perfect garden”: Miyabe Kingo and the making of a botanist in Hokkaido, 1860–89
abstract: This paper examines the importance of places and affects in the formative years of Japanese botanist Miyabe Kingo (1860–1951) and the transformation of Hokkaido, the northern island of Japan, into a “Perfect Garden.” It begins by showing how the Meiji government and American advisors invoked the climatic similarities between Hokkaido and Northeastern America in the colonization of the island and the establishment of the Sapporo Agricultural College (SAC). William S. Clark (1826–86), the first president of the SAC, brought a distinct combination of New Botany and Christianity to the first cohort of students, who then influenced Miyabe in the second cohort. Although Clark’s teaching situated evolutionary theory and Christian faith in perfect harmony, with his departure, the students were left to navigate their professional and religious identities. Miyabe’s passion for botany was therefore intertwined not only with the state’s colonial project but repeated emotional and spiritual struggles. This paper aims to approach the role places and affects played in the making of a botanist when the professionalization of the field had just begun and to elucidate the mutual influences between identity formation and place-making.

title: A “Modern” Corporeality of Imperialism: Intersectionality of Equine and Human Bodies in Meiji (1868–1912) Japan
abstract: This paper delves into the ways in which the subjugation of the equine body was intricately linked to the discipline of the human body in early Meiji Japan (1868–1912). Horse racing, in conjunction with the notion of a modern corporeality, played a significant role in Japan’s pursuit to establish itself as an imperial power following the imposition of unequal treaties. The violence of colonialism instigated a modernization process aligned with Western standards of power, body, and governance, demanding the transformation of both human and equine corporeality. This process essentially aimed to prepare individuals to effectively partake in “modern” pursuits, especially warfare. Horse racing, in this context, was not merely entertainment but a tool of imperial nation-building, providing both a financial base and a training ground for cavalry horses, while forming part of the westernization initiative that directly contributed to Japan’s transition into an imperial power. The discipline of the equine body in horse racing relied fundamentally on the rider’s ability to regulate and control their own body; thus, this interlinked discipline of human and horse was integral to the broader project of imperialism. Accordingly, a comprehensive understanding of the interrelated nature of all forms of violence is imperative to the study of imperialism and the pursuit of liberation.

title: The concept of Buddhism in nihonga art based on the work of Yokoyama Taikan
abstract: During the Meiji period (1868—1912), Japan faced serious challenges. Amidst rapid Westernization and modernization, the country was forced to re-invent its national identity. At the same time, the government made Shintō the state religion, which contributed to the rise of anti-Buddhist sentiment and the development of the haibutsu kishaku 廃仏毀釈 (“eradicating Buddhism and abolishing Shakyamuni”) movement. This policy led to the destruction of temples, statues, and paintings, threatening centuries-old cultural heritage. Then, in response to the adoption of European-style painting yōga 洋画, the nihonga 日本画, or Japanese-style painting movement emerged. It sought to preserve and reinterpret traditional art in a contemporary context. One of the key figures of this school was Yokoyama Taikan, who studied under Okakura Kakuzō. Thanks to his teacher’s influence, the young artist perceived Buddhism as one of the foundations of Japanese culture. In his work, Taikan did not simply copy ancient works but instead sought to develop a new visual language to express traditions and philosophical concepts. A significant milestone was his trip to India in 1903, where the artist was inspired to create works with Indian motifs, which served as impetus for the further development of modern Japanese painting. In his works, Yokoyama Taikan placed great emphasis on a profound understanding of Buddhist philosophy, which is reflected in such outstanding works as Selflessness ( Muga 無我) and Metempsychosis ( Seisei ruten 生々流転). Furthermore, the artist made a significant contribution to the development of artistic expression in modern art as one of the founders of the “hazy style” ( mōrōtai 朦朧体). This technique conveyed the atmosphere and spiritual depth without the use of clear contours. Thus, Yokoyama Taikan was one of the leading nihonga artists who actively engaged with traditions, particularly Buddhist themes. In his works, he strove to find a subtle balance between cultural heritage and innovation, which lay at the heart of the formation of Japan’s national identity at the time.

title: Nampo Joshi: Reconstructing the Life of the Woman Artist Behind Whistler’s Old Battersea Bridge
abstract: This paper investigates the identity and circumstances of Nampo Joshi (南芳女史) (Ōzawa Nampo 大澤南芳, b. 1845; born Takei Tsuru), the woman artist who painted the kachō-ga (bird-and-flower painting) affixed to the reverse of James McNeill Whistler’s Blue and Silver: Old Battersea Bridge (1871/1873, The Hunterian, University of Glasgow). Completed in 1867, as the Edo period ended, Nampo’s work reached Europe with remarkable speed, raising the question of how a painting by a Japanese woman came into Whistler’s possession. Few historical documents directly pertaining to Nampo survive. However, she was the wife of the painter Ōzawa Nankoku (大澤南谷, 1844–?), and a systematic examination of records related to him—land registers, official gazettes, periodicals, exhibition catalogues, and diaries—reveals that the couple established themselves in Nihonbashi, the commercial centre of Tokyo. This broader archival investigation reconstructs who Nampo was: the socio-economic standing she and her husband achieved and the ways in which they extended their endeavours well beyond the traditional boundaries of their craft—participating energetically in the civic life of the new capital, in the exhibition culture of the Meiji period, and in educational and philanthropic activities. Crucially, the study demonstrates that masters deeply involved in Rangaku (Dutch Studies) networks advocating Japan’s opening to the world trained both artists and argues that this progressive intellectual milieu may provide essential context for understanding the swift acceptance of Nampo’s work in Europe.

title: Inadvertent Restraint: Theory of Rising Great Power Underexpansion
abstract: Why do rising great powers sometimes pass up cheap territorial expansion under an open window of opportunity? Existing explanations, rooted in calculated restraint, weak state capacity, or the absence of a mobilizing ideology, cannot account for cases in which a state possesses ample capability and will yet declines to act. This article develops a theory of inadvertent restraint. During early, state-led industrialization, financing rapid economic growth compels the formation of internalist, anti-imperialist coalitions whose parochial stake lies in domestic construction rather than foreign expansion. These coalitions capture the fiscal and administrative machinery of the state and manufacture false pessimism about the value of expansion, producing a systematic misperception of cumulativity rather than a considered judgment against it. The theory is tested through a crucial case of within-case variation in Meiji Japan, whose restraint toward Korea in 1873 gave way to calculated aggression by 1910, a less permissive boundary case in the United States annexation of Hawaii, and a plausibility probe from reform-era China.

title: Existential Deconstruction of Sovereign Character Identity in Koyoharu Gotouge’s Visual Narrative: From the Heterotopia of Yoshiwara to the Manifesto of the Shiraume
abstract: The subject of this research is a comprehensive existential-semiotic deconstruction of the sovereign identity and ontological being of the popular character Ume in Koyoharu Gotouge's Japanese graphic novel "Demon Slayer". The author thoroughly examines such critical aspects as the specific century-long existence of the literary heroine within the specialized space of high sociocultural density and her subsequent attainment of absolute sovereign autonomy contrary to the explicit pragmatic intent of the work's author. Special attention is paid to the systematic analysis of the fictional character's unique existential experience, the process of forming her free choice within the metaphysical space of Limbo, and her functioning as an emancipated conceptual subject of contemporary mass culture. The methodological framework of the study relies on an operational synergy of Jacques Lacan’s structural psychoanalysis and John Austin’s speech act theory. This analytical instrumentation is integrated into the context of Umberto Eco’s semiotics, G.W.F. Hegel’s dialectics, Gilles Deleuze’s conceptual character philosophy, and Nikolai Berdyaev’s metaphysics of freedom. The scientific novelty lies in the fact that the excessive historical context of Yoshiwara during the Kasei, Meiji, and Taisho eras is conceptualized for the first time as a hyper-dense substrate determining the structural autonomy of a character. The original theoretical construct of the "Century-Old Observer" is proposed here. The main conclusions reveal a profound metatextual error of the work's demiurge through the prism of Hegel's "cunning of reason" and prove the heroine's transformation into a metaphysical being – Shiraume. This phenomenon turns Ume into the epicenter of an existential catastrophe, initiating text destruction within Eco's semiotic paradigm.

title: Modernization of Education in Tokyo during the Meiji Era: The Metropolitan School and the University of Tokyo as Channels for the Formation of a New Imperial Elite
abstract: The beginning of the Meiji era (1868–1912) initiated a series of complementary large-scale reforms aimed not only at transforming the political and socio-economic system of Japan but also at modernizing Japanese society itself. After the renaming of Edo to Tokyo and the establishment of the imperial court and main state institutions in the city, the former center of shogunate power began its transformation into a new imperial capital. One of the directions of the ongoing reforms was the restructuring of the educational system that had been established in previous years. The article is dedicated to the modernization of education in Tokyo during the Meiji era and explores the interrelationship between the emergence of mass elementary schooling, the development of the University of Tokyo, and the formation of a new imperial elite. The aim of the work is to determine how state educational policy was implemented in the capital and depended on the material capabilities of families, local funding, and the everyday strategies of students. The research was conducted using problem-chronological and source-critic methods. The source base included the "Gakusei" decree of 1872, the Statute of the Imperial University of 1886, materials from the Tokyo Educational Society, student guides, literary evidence, and cartographic materials; statistical data on school attendance were also used. It was found that the rapid expansion of the school network did not ensure immediate universal coverage: at the national level, in 1873, 28.1% of children attended elementary school, and by 1878 this figure had risen to 41.3%; there remained a significant gap between boys and girls. The functioning of schools depended on the means of parents and local communities, the use of temples, private homes, and other temporary premises, as well as educational efforts among urban residents. It was demonstrated that the University of Tokyo trained staff for the government and science, but access to it was determined not only by abilities but also by socio-economic resources. By the beginning of the 20th century, education under external patronage was complemented by an independent model of kugaku: students combined studies with part-time work, utilized new forms of transport, and adapted to urban life. It was concluded that, despite the persistent inequality in access, educational modernization encompassed all levels of education, and the formation of a new elite began in schools and continued at the university and in the everyday life of the capital.

title: The Demise of the Owari Domain School Meirindō during the Late Edo and Meiji Restoration Transformation
abstract: This study examines the trajectory followed by domain school education during Japan's transition from the early modern to the modern era, using the Owari domain school, the Meirindō 明倫堂, as a case study.In particular, to the best of my knowledge, little previous research has addressed the fate of the temple-school system, which integrated a teaching venue for Chinese Learning education (Kangaku 漢学) -the core component of the curriculum for training mid-ranking samurai comprising the administrative leadership class -with a shrine where the Sekiten 釈奠 or Sekisai 釈菜 sacrifice to Confucius was performed.This article investigates how this temple-school system, which had remained the standard design of Bakufu and domain schools throughout the early modern period, was dismantled during the turmoils of the late Edo period and the Meiji Restoration, by examining specific developments in the Meirindō, an early pioneer of this system.Developments in Owari offer an important perspective in understanding characteristics of domain school education in early modern Japan overall.In Owari we find early on the forerunner of the temple-school system that would later become such a distinctive feature of early modern domain schools.The temple-school system, originally the design of official schools in China during the Tang dynasty, combined a teaching hall with a shrine to the Sage (Confucius) .Educationally, it integrated instruction in the Chinese classics with the performance of the Sekiten or Sekisai -the school ritual venerating Confucius, the founding sage of the Confucian tradition.In Japan, the construction of the Confucius temple (Senseiden 先聖殿) at Hayashi Razan's school at Shinobuoka (Shinobugaoka juku 忍岡塾) in 1632, one of the earliest schools in Edo, and the Sekisai ceremony first held there in 1633, were made possible with the substantial support of Tokugawa Yoshinao 徳 川 義 直 (1601-1650, r. 1610-1650) , the first lord of Owari, who provided the shrine building itself, a Confucius statue image, and ritual utensils.Furthermore, Yoshinao himself performed the Sekisai ceremony during the Kan'ei era (1624-1644) and established a school that would ultimately evolve into the Meirindō.Thus, the establishment of the temple-school system and the Sekisai ceremony in Owari were pioneering examples in early modern Japan, a prototype of 〔Article〕 -1 -千葉商大紀要 第 64 巻 第 1 号(2026 年 7 月)pp.1-23

title: MEIJI JAPAN IN THE OTTOMAN IMAGINARY: YUSUF OSMAN
abstract: Published in Salonica in 1910, first as a serial in the newspaper Zaman and subsequently as an independent treatise, Yusuf Osman's Japonya: Ahvâl-i Hâzırası ve Sûret-i Tekâmülü (Japan: Its Present Condition and Its Path of Development) constitutes one of the rare and systematic examples through which the late Ottoman-Islamic world constructed its imaginary of Meiji Japan. This article subjects the treatise to a critical historical reading, examining how the text interweaves themes of environmental determinism, the instrumentalization of religious belief for national discipline, an elitist paradigm of modernization, hostility toward labor movements and socialism, a regime of gender relations, and urban description. The study argues that Yusuf Osman does not merely describe Japan but transforms it into a normative program of "discipline" for Ottoman-Islamic society a program centered not on the free individual but on the figure of the "self-sacrificing nation". Read as an extension of the broader Ottoman-Japanese intellectual encounter (the Ertuğrul frigate disaster, the Russo-Japanese War, and Abdürreşid İbrahim's travels), the text exposes a shared predicament of non-Western modernization projects: the tension between the aspiration to modernize and an organicist, authoritarian vision of society.

title: Russian orthodox mission in Japan
abstract: In the Meiji era when Japan took the path of modernization along Western patterns, the country became open to Christian influences. The Russian orthodox church began its missionary work with sending Nicholas to Japan. In contrast to the missionary activities of other (Western) Christian confessions, the history of the Russian orthodox mission to Japan presents a lacuna. The task of the Russian orthodox mission was not only to convert Japanese to Christian orthodox belief in competition to Western Christian confessions, but also to spread the Russian language and culture, and to seed a positive image of Imperial Russia among the Japanese population. It is worth mentioning that despite of all Russo-Japanese constraints in the Twentieth century, i.e. from the Russo-Japanese War of 1904/1905 and the dispute over the Kuriles after 1945, the legacy of the Russian orthodox mission in Japan is permanent. Until today there exists an independent Japanese orthodox community. The nucleus of the Russian orthodox mission was the Resurrection Church as part of the Russian consulate in Hakodate, opened in 1858 after the signing of the Treaty of Shimoda (1855) which initiated the diplomatic relations between Russia and Japan. The first task of the church was to provide orthodox services to the Russian diplomatic staff. This was the task of Nikolai (Nicholas) Kasatkin who arrived in 1861. From the very beginning Kasatkin showed a great affinity to Japan, he learnt Japanese and he thoroughly studied the Japanese culture. By this he gained a deep understanding of Japanese mentality and mores. Due to the animosity of the Japanese government toward foreign Christian missionaries in the 1870s, Kasatkin began to train native Japanese orthodox preachers. This was the beginning of the native Japanese orthodox community in Japan. In 1874 there were 900 Japanese orthodox believers, about 100 in Tokyo, about 300 in Hakodate, and about 500 in Sendai. Four years later there were 4,215 Japanese orthodox converts. The Russian orthodox church (ROC) showed a different approach to her missionary work in Japan than the Roman Catholics and Protestants. The ROC used native preachers to spread Russian orthodoxy. Additionally, the ROC aimed at missioning households, not individuals, as Japanese wives were attracted by religious education. In this way, Kasatkin founded a women school. The problem of the Russian orthodox mission in Japan was the lack of sufficient funding by the Russian imperial government. The Roman Catholics received twenty-six and the Protestants fifteen times more money for the missionary activities.
